title: Splitting a name on the last space doesn't find the surname — it finds the last WORD
assumption: The text after the last space in a full name is the surname.

input.description: A 'full name' text field being split into given/surname for a database or a form, using the common 'last word = surname' heuristic.

what_goes_wrong: The surname field ends up holding just "Berg", and "van der" — which is part of the actual family name "van der Berg" — gets silently folded into the given-name field instead.
why: Splitting on the last whitespace boundary only knows about whitespace, not about which words belong to the family name. Dutch, German, and other surnames routinely include lowercase particles (van, der, von, de) that are grammatically and legally part of the surname, not separate given names, and a position-based split has no way to know where the surname actually starts.
affects: any 'split full name on whitespace' form handler

repros.code:
def naive_split(full_name):
    given, surname = full_name.rsplit(" ", 1)
    return given, surname

print(naive_split("Joost van der Berg"))

fix: Collect given-name and family-name as separate fields entered directly by the person instead of inferring the split from word position; if you must infer it, maintain an explicit list of known lowercase surname particles to fold into the family-name side.

sources.title: Patrick McKenzie: Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names

test_cases.note: Check whether your surname field comes out as 'Berg' or 'van der Berg' — most systems get this wrong.
